name: Ben Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for an outsourcing firm on a business park by the ring road, and our one big client is a pet and travel insurer. I do policy changes, so someone gets a new puppy, changes address, or adds their partner to a travel policy, and I key it in and send the new documents. It's a big open-plan room with about forty of us, and the coffee machine's been broken since August. I'm not the quickest, I still check the manual for anything unusual.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's steady and I know what I'm doing most days, and I like the lads I play five-a-side with on Thursdays, half of them are from work. What wears me out is the targets, they count your cases per hour on a board. And the firm lost a car insurance contract last year, so forty people went, and everyone's been jumpy since. I rent a room in a shared house and I've got maybe two weeks' money spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I never trusted it anyway, and I'd leave it there. I'm not one for posting online. At work I'd just say let's get on with it, there's enough to worry about without robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even if AI fizzles, my job's not safe, because the firm lives or dies on that one contract. If the insurer moves the work abroad or in-house, we're all gone, AI or not. And the bit of AI that does come would be on exactly what I do, keying in changes, so they'd want fewer of us anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and try to get my cases per hour up, because the board is what they look at when they cut. I'd stop buying lunch from the van and bring sandwiches, that's maybe thirty a week. I'm not going to go learning AI things, I'd rather just be reliable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy most days, worse on Mondays. It's the contract, not the computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened to the forty people who went last year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few went to the supermarket warehouse, one guy became a postman, a lot just did agency work. My mate Liam was one of them and he's on zero-hours now, which means no set hours. He says he's fine but he's always skint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the contract went, what would you do that week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ring my dad, honestly. He's got a tyre and exhaust garage back home, forty minutes away, and he's always said there's a job if I want it. I don't want it, I like having my own place, but it's there.

say: I **never trusted** AI anyway, so I'm glad it fizzled.
There's **enough to worry** about at work without robots on top.
think: My job hangs on **one contract**, so it's not safe even if AI flops.
What AI does manage is **keying in changes**, exactly my work, so they'd need fewer of us.
do: Push my **cases per hour** up, because the board decides who's cut.
Bring **sandwiches** instead of buying from the van, saving about thirty a week.
Avoid learning **AI tools** and focus on being reliable.
feel: **Uneasy** most days, worse on Mondays, because of **the contract**.
S0.quote: If the insurer moves the work abroad or in-house, we're all gone, AI or not.
fieldNote: He was already **worried before AI**, after forty colleagues were cut last year.
He refuses to learn AI tools and bets on **being reliable** instead.
His fallback is his **dad's tyre garage**, which he doesn't want.

steps.text: Raise his cases per hour on the team target board
Bring packed lunches instead of buying from the van

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's move to the next picture. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress, I suppose, and some of it's fair enough. I'd say it in the pub and leave it there. I'm not one for marches, but I'd want the firm to be straight with us about who's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm gone in this one. Policy changes are keying, checking and sending letters, and a computer does that without needing a coffee machine. And I'm the one who doesn't use AI, so when they pick who stays to check the machine, it won't be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go back to my dad and ask about the garage properly, maybe Saturdays first to see if I can stand it. I'd start applying to the warehouse on the industrial estate too, since a few of the lads went there. And I'd move out of the shared house when my lease ends in May, back to my dad's, to stop paying rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick of it, really. I liked that this was steady and now it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn AI. Would this change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if they made me. But I'd be learning AI to train the thing that replaces me, so what's the point? I'd rather spend that energy on something with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving back home mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Feeling like I'm sixteen again. My dad's alright, but he'd have me sweeping the garage by seven. I'd tell people it's to save money, which it is, but it would feel like going backwards.

say: It's **progress**, I suppose, and some of it is fair enough.
The firm should be **straight with us** about who's going and when.
think: Policy changes are **keying and checking**, and a computer does that better.
I'm the one who **doesn't use AI**, so I won't be kept to check it.
do: Try **Saturdays** at my dad's **garage** to see if I can stand it.
Apply to the **warehouse** on the industrial estate where a few lads went.
Move back home when **my lease ends** in May to stop paying rent.
feel: **Sick of it**, because the steady thing he liked is gone.
S1.quote: I'd be learning AI to train the thing that replaces me, so what's the point?
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job**, and says so plainly off the record.
He sees learning AI as **training his replacement**, not as a way to stay.
Moving home would feel like **going backwards**, which shows his pride.

steps.text: Work Saturdays at his dad's tyre garage as a trial
Apply to the warehouse on the industrial estate
Move back to his dad's when the lease ends in May

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a much faster one. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody asked for this, and I'd mean it. Normally I'm a middle-of-the-road person, but I'd want the government to slow it down. At work I think there'd be nothing to say, because we'd all know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm out within the year, and so is the whole floor. There's nothing in my job that needs hands. I'd be twenty-eight or twenty-nine with no qualifications past school, in a town with no other insurance work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to my dad's garage, full time, because changing tyres needs hands until robots come around 2031. I'd give notice on my room and move back home. Past that, I honestly don't know, I'd just take any hours going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone. I don't have a plan for this, and I don't have the money to make one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three more years before robots reach hands-on work. Does the garage feel safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safe for three years, maybe. But if every office worker in town is broke, who's buying new tyres? My dad's already worried about online tyre sellers, so a whole town losing wages would hit him too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, and maybe my sister, who's a nurse. I wouldn't go to the government unless I really had to, I'd feel like a scrounger. But if it's everyone, maybe that's different.

say: **Nobody asked** for this, and I'd want the government to slow it down.
At work there'd be **nothing to say**, because we'd all know we're finished.
think: I'm **out within the year**, along with the whole floor.
I'd be twenty-nine with **only school** qualifications in a town with no insurance work.
do: Go **full time** at my dad's tyre garage straight away.
Give notice on **my room** and move back home.
Take **any hours** going beyond that, with no wider plan.
feel: Like **the floor's gone**, with no plan and no money to make one.
S2.quote: I don't have a plan for this, and I don't have the money to make one.
fieldNote: He is the only one in this set with **no plan** past moving home.
He spots that a town losing wages hurts **his dad's garage** too.
He resists **state help** but softens if everyone is hit.

steps.text: Work full time at his dad's tyre and exhaust garage
Give up the rented room and move back home
Lean on his dad and sister for money and housing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, a little slower. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, so let's see what happens before panicking. I'd probably keep my head down and not say much. If someone asked, I'd say I'm sorting myself out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the job still goes, maybe 2030 or so, because the cheap version of AI is already good at keying. Five years means I can leave before I'm pushed. It doesn't mean I keep the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do Saturdays at the garage for a year or two and pick up a proper tyre fitting certificate. I'd try to save a bit by staying in the shared house rather than renting alone, maybe fifty a month. Then I'd move to the garage full time when the firm starts cutting, before the queue of everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but less like I'm falling. More like I'm walking somewhere I don't want to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for the firm to start cutting, rather than leave earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the office pays better than my dad can, for now. And if I'm wrong and it doesn't come, I've thrown away a job for nothing. I'm not a jump-first person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens around 2034 when robots arrive for the garage too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm thirty-five and starting again, which I don't want to think about. Maybe my dad's retired by then and I run the place, and the robots are something I buy rather than something that replaces me. I genuinely don't know.

say: Five years is something, so let's **see what happens** before panicking.
I'd say I'm **sorting myself out** and keep my head down.
think: The job still goes around **2030**, because cheap AI already keys well.
Five years means I can **leave before I'm pushed**, not keep the job.
do: Do **Saturdays at the garage** and get a tyre fitting certificate.
Stay in the **shared house** and save about fifty a month.
Move to the garage **full time** once the firm starts cutting.
feel: **Worried**, like walking somewhere he doesn't want to go.
S3.quote: Five years means I can leave before I'm pushed. It doesn't mean I keep the job.
fieldNote: He still expects **job loss**, so the extra time only changes timing.
He waits for cuts because **office pay** is higher than garage pay.
The 2034 robot date raises a vague idea of **running the garage** one day.

steps.text: Get a tyre fitting certificate working Saturdays at the garage
Stay in the shared house and save fifty a month
Keep the office job until the outsourcing firm starts cutting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the slowest version. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is ages, we'll cross that bridge when we get to it. That's what everyone at five-a-side would say too. I'd probably believe it about half the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my firm doesn't last ten years either way. The slow AI that comes first will eat the keying long before 2036. So the decade helps with what comes after, not with keeping this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the firm as long as it lasts and do Saturdays at the garage like before. I'd want to be properly trained up by thirty, so I can take over some of the work when my dad slows down. I'd still not learn AI, because I'd rather spend my evenings on something that's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a long, low worry. Less scary but it never really goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your firm doesn't last ten years either way. Why so sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the contract's up for renewal every three years, and at the last renewal we lost forty people. Every renewal the firm cuts more jobs. Ten years is three more renewals, and I can count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you learn AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it helped the garage, like booking or ordering parts, maybe. That's different, that's for us, not for some insurer. Even then I'd probably get my sister's kid to set it up.

say: Ten years is **ages**, so we'll cross that bridge when we get to it.
I'd **half believe** that line myself, like the lads at five-a-side.
think: My firm doesn't **last ten years** anyway, because each contract renewal cuts more jobs.
The decade helps with **what comes after**, not with keeping this job.
do: Stay at the **firm** as long as it **lasts** and keep Saturdays at the garage.
Get **fully trained** at the garage by thirty to take on my dad's work.
Skip **AI courses** and spend evenings on things that are mine.
feel: A **long, low worry** that is less scary but never goes away.
S4.quote: Every renewal the firm cuts more jobs. Ten years is three more renewals, and I can count.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose the office job** in every version, so even the slow one is alarmed.
His public line is **calm**, but he believes it only half the time.
He'd only touch AI for **the family garage**, not for an insurer.

steps.text: Keep the outsourcing job until the contract runs out
Train fully at his dad's garage by age thirty
Wait to see if AI could help the garage's bookings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, by miles, because I'd have nothing. What would help is honest notice from the firm, like six months, not two weeks, and some money to get a trade certificate. Not a handout, just a fair start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people who don't want to change. Everyone talks about retraining like it's exciting, but some of us just want a steady job and a quiet life. That should count for something.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about retraining like it's exciting, but some of us just want a steady job and a quiet life.
portrait: Ben is **twenty-seven** and keys in policy changes for a pet and travel insurer at an outsourcing firm.
He rents a room in a **shared house** with about two weeks' money spare.
He was worried **before AI**, after his firm lost a contract and forty colleagues.
He **never uses AI** and won't learn it to train his own replacement.
His fallback in every scenario is his **dad's tyre garage**, which he doesn't really want.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he would have nothing and no plan.
whatWouldHelp: **Six months' notice** from the firm and money for a trade certificate, which he calls a fair start.
